  • Remove outliers
In [43]:
num_df = df.select_dtypes(include='number')

Q1 = num_df.quantile(0.25)
Q3 = num_df.quantile(0.75)
IQR = Q3 - Q1

df = df[~((num_df < (Q1 - 1.5 * IQR)) |(num_df > (Q3 + 1.5 * IQR))).any(axis=1)]

df.ApplicantIncome = np.sqrt(df.ApplicantIncome)
df.CoapplicantIncome = np.sqrt(df.CoapplicantIncome)
df.LoanAmount = np.sqrt(df.LoanAmount)

Documentation¶

Summary

In this project we are classifying people as being eligible or not for a loan.

The dataset we are using has 13 variables: 1 id, 8 categorical and 4 numerical variables. We are trying to classify on the Loan Status variable.

We are also trying to determine the best model for this task, so we will be using 7 different models which will be compared in terms of accuracy.

Implementation

First thing was to explore the data from the dataset to better understand what we are working with.

During the exploration there are multiple variables which are unbalanced (ex. Gender, Credit History or even Loan Status).

Next, we explore correlations between the variables. We can see a positive correlation between Loan Amount and Applicant Income.

It is important to also determine the amount of outliers for each variable. We can see that for Applicant Income, Coapplicant Income and Loan Amount there are a considerable number of outliers.

Next comes the data preprocessing. First is the data imputation, which substitutes an estimated value for missing values in the dataset.

At this point we are also removing the outliers.

Last notable thing to do is to balance the dataset. As mentioned before, the Loan Status variable, which is used in our classification, is unbalenced. To fix that, we are using the SMOTE technique so that Loan Status can be balanced. This is done by artificially inserting entries in the dataset with estimated values based on other entries. This is important to avoid bias in the models.

Lastly, the data is normalized and split in training and testing sets.

Results

The models used, with their accuracies are the following:

  • Logistic Regression - 80.62%
  • KNN - 82.95%
  • SVM - 82.95%
  • Gaussian Naive Bayes - 65.89%
  • Decision Tree - 82.95%
  • Random Forest - 84.50%
  • Gradient Boost - 79.07%

As a result, the best performing model is Random Forest, achieving 84.5%, closely followed by 3 models achieving the same accuracy of 82.95% (KNN, SVM, Decision Tree).

The worst performing model is the Gaussian Naive Bayes, achieving only 65.89% accuracy.
